name: Percentage increase

summary: The Percentage increase calculator takes the numbers you enter and reports increase (%) immediately. It is free to use, needs no account, and shows the working rather than just the answer. That makes it useful for a homework check, a spreadsheet build or a bit of mental arithmetic you want to confirm. The results leave the screen the moment you edit a field; press Calculate and they come back updated, so a single changed input shows its own effect.

sections.title: How does the Percentage increase calculator work?
sections.html:
The Percentage increase calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports increase (%) in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (increase or decrease?); then you type in the figures it asks for.

Press Calculate and the page works through the equation with the values you supplied and derives the rest; it then keeps up with you as you correct a typo.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: What do you need to enter?
sections.html:
• Pick the option that matches your case — 2 options, such as increase and decrease. The choice changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier, so it is worth reading the options carefully.
  • A plain number with no unit attached.

1 field on this form is a choice rather than a number. Those choices decide which version of the calculation applies, so they are worth setting before you worry about the digits.

sections.title: The formula behind the Percentage increase calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Increase (%)=(-initial value + final value) ÷ initial value
Initial value=-final value − Initial value + final value
Increase (%)=(-initial value + final value) ÷ the absolute value of (initial value)
Initial value=-final value ÷ (decrease (%) − 1)

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

Results are rounded for display but computed at full precision, so chaining one result into the next does not accumulate error. Very large and very small numbers switch to scientific notation rather than printing a run of zeros.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Percentage increase calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Checking a homework answer before you hand it in
  • Building the same calculation into a spreadsheet and wanting a reference value
  • Settling an argument about a number with a quick, traceable result

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.
  • Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

sections.title: What are the limits worth knowing?
sections.html:
Every tool draws a boundary somewhere. For the Percentage increase calculator, these are the ones that matter:

  • The 1 drop-down on this page offers a fixed list of cases. A value that is not on the list cannot be entered, and the nearest option is not always a good substitute.
  • The unit chips cover the units listed on the page. A historical or regional unit that is missing can still be used by converting it to a listed unit first.
  • The calculator reports what the relationship implies; it does not judge whether the inputs themselves are sensible, so a figure that is out by a factor of ten will produce an answer that is out by the same factor.

faq.q: What does the Percentage increase calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns increase (%). Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Percentage increase calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for a few values, which is 2 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter increase (%) in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Increase (%) opens in percent and the chip beside it offers 6 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There is one choice to make (1 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

faq.q: Is the Percentage increase calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
